comparisons.peer_summary: The bank evaluates VaR accuracy via daily backtesting, comparing one-day VaR results against a regulatory-defined subset of trading revenue, expecting loss excesses to align with the 99% confidence level (approx. 1-3 per year).
comparisons.comparison: Both Goldman Sachs (GS) and Bank of America (BAC) disclose the frequency of Value-at-Risk (VaR) exceptions (losses exceeding the VaR threshold) to validate their risk models, though they utilize different confidence levels and have different observed exception counts. GS reports 2 exceptions in 2024 and 1 in 2023 using a 95% confidence level, linking frequency to its business model's revenue mix (positive vs. loss days). BAC uses a 99% confidence level, expecting 2-3 exceptions annually, and notes that observed exceptions can vary from the statistical expectation due to market volatility differences during the lookback period compared to the historical data used for the VaR calculation.

sentences.text: Net losses incurred on a single day for such positions exceeded our 95% one-day VaR (i.e., a VaR exception) on two occasions during 2024 and on one occasion during 2023.

During periods in which we have significantly more positive net revenue days than net revenue loss days, we expect to have fewer VaR exceptions because, under normal conditions, our business model generally produces positive net revenues.
We expect the frequency of trading losses in excess of VaR to be in line with the confidence level of the VaR statistic being tested.
For example, with a 99 percent confidence level, we expect one trading loss in excess of VaR every 100 days or between two to three trading losses in excess of VaR over the course of a year.

comparisons.peer_topic: Expected Back-Testing Exceptions and Market Condition Sensitivity
comparisons.peer_summary: Citi expects two to three days per year where buy-and-hold losses exceed Regulatory VaR at a 99% confidence level, though fewer exceptions are expected under stable conditions due to conservative model calibration; unstable market conditions could increase exceptions.
comparisons.comparison: Like GS, Citi (C) discusses the expected frequency of VaR exceptions relative to market stability and model calibration, but operates at a 99% confidence level versus GS's 95%. GS states that fewer exceptions are expected during periods with significantly more positive net revenue days, while Citi expects 2-3 exceptions per year at 99% confidence but anticipates fewer exceptions under stable market conditions due to conservative model calibration. Both firms acknowledge that market conditions (volatility/stability) drive the deviation from expected exception rates.

sentences.text: During periods in which we have significantly more positive net revenue days than net revenue loss days, we expect to have fewer VaR exceptions because, under normal conditions, our business model generally produces positive net revenues.
Based on a 99% confidence level, Citi would expect two to three days in any one year where buy-and-hold losses exceed the Regulatory VaR.

Given the conservative calibration of Citi's VaR model (as a result of taking the greater of short- and long-term volatilities and fat-tail scaling of volatilities), Citi would expect fewer exceptions under normal and stable market conditions.

comparisons.peer_summary: For the 12 months ended December 31, 2024, the Firm posted backtesting gains on 179 of 260 days and observed eight VaR backtesting exceptions, three of which occurred in the three months ended December 31, 2024. Firmwide backtesting loss days may differ from Fixed Income or Equity Markets loss days due to differences in position populations and excluded revenue components.
comparisons.comparison: Both GS and JPMorgan (JPM) report specific counts of VaR backtesting exceptions for the fiscal year 2024, serving as empirical evidence of model performance. GS reported 2 exceptions in 2024, while JPM reported 8 exceptions. JPM explicitly distinguishes its backtesting loss days from 'loss days' recorded in its Markets business unit revenue, noting that backtesting includes VaR positions and excludes certain revenue components, whereas GS links its exception frequency directly to the ratio of positive to negative net revenue days inherent in its business model.

sentences.text: Net losses incurred on a single day for such positions exceeded our 95% one-day VaR (i.e., a VaR exception) on two occasions during 2024 and on one occasion during 2023.

For the 12 months ended December 31, 2024, the Firm posted backtesting gains on 179 of the 260 days, and observed eight VaR backtesting exceptions, of which three were in the three months ended December 31, 2024.

Firmwide backtesting loss days can differ from the loss days for which Fixed Income Markets and Equity Markets posted losses, as disclosed in CIB Markets revenue, as the population of positions which comprise each metric are different and due to the exclusion of certain components of total net revenue in backtesting gains and losses as described above.
